Texture synthesis, drawn

Q4 runs Q2 backwards. In Q2 you turned an image into feature statistics and compared them. Here you fix the statistics of an exemplar and search for a new image that has the same ones, by gradient descent on the pixels. A texture is an image that is fully described by such statistics: what patterns occur, and nothing about where. Which statistics you match (mean and variance, or the Gram matrix) decides what survives.

1 · the idea

Freeze the network, measure the exemplar, then move the pixels

Three things are different from training a network. The weights never change. The thing being optimised is the image itself. And the target is not an image but a set of numbers measured from the exemplar's feature maps.

Where this sits in your notes. Differentiating a scalar with respect to the input image is the saliency computation W5 §5.11.1, and optimising an input instead of the weights is how the notes describe activation maximisation W5 §5.10.5. The update is the usual θ ← θ − η ∂L/∂θ W4 Eq. 4 with the pixels playing the role of θ, and the gradient comes from the chain rule through every layer W2 §5.2. Texture statistics and Gram matrices are not in the notes, so they are built from scratch below. The Normalization module in your cell exists because “preprocessing … normalization” must match the checkpoint W5 §5.1.5: (img − mean) / std per channel, as the first layer of the model so gradients flow through it.

2 · question 4a · three statistics

Mean, variance and Gram: three ways to forget where things are

A layer's output for one image is a tensor F of shape C × H × W: C channels, each an H × W map. Write P = H·W for the number of positions. All three statistics sum over positions, so moving content around cannot change them.

mean μc = (1/P) Σp F[c,p] how strongly channel c fires on average C numbers, shape 1×C×1×1
var vc = (1/P) Σp (F[c,p] − μc)² how much it varies over the image C numbers, shape 1×C×1×1
gram G[i,j] = (1/(C·P)) Σp F[i,p]·F[j,p] do channels i and j fire together? C×C numbers
link C · G[c,c] = (1/P) Σp F[c,p]² = vc + μc² the Gram diagonal already holds mean and variance, combined

“Along the 3rd and 4th dimension, keep all dimensions” in your docstring means: average over H and W only, and keep the result as 1×C×1×1 rather than a flat vector. The Gram needs F reshaped to C rows and P columns first; it is F·Fᵀ, the same matrix as in Q2 mode 4 and XᵀX in Q1 W1 §3.1. Check the normaliser against the Gram you wrote for Q2 and use the same one.

A toy layer you can scramble

Three channels on a 6×6 grid. A and B are the same stripes, so they always fire together. C fires in blobs. Two ways to scramble, and they are the whole difference between the two losses.

3 · question 4b · optimising the pixels

Start from noise, follow the gradient until the statistics match

A StyleLoss module sits after a chosen layer, compares the current statistics with the stored target, saves the squared difference in self.loss and passes its input on unchanged. The total loss is the sum over the chosen layers.

gram L = Σlayers mean( (G(x) − G(s))² )
mean_var L = Σlayers mean( (μ(x) − μ(s))² ) + mean( (v(x) − v(s))² )
gradient ∂L/∂F = (4 / (C·P)) · (G(x) − G(s)) · F for the Gram term, up to the mean's constant; then back through conv, ReLU, pool to x
step L-BFGS: build a curvature estimate from recent gradients, take a Newton-like step with a line search W2 §6.2, §6.4

Your notes: “Quasi-Newton methods such as L-BFGS approximate curvature from gradient/parameter changes” W2 §6.4. A full Newton step needs the Hessian, which for a 256×256×3 image would be a 196,608 × 196,608 matrix; L-BFGS keeps only a handful of recent gradient pairs. In PyTorch it re-evaluates the loss several times per step, which is why it takes a closure function that zeroes the gradient, runs the model, sums the losses, calls backward and returns the loss. The target tensors are detached: they are constants.

4 · questions 4d and 4e

What each statistic can reproduce

Every exemplar, synthesised twice from the same noise. Under each result: how far its conv1_1 statistics ended from the exemplar's, as a relative error (0% = identical). “Co-occurrence” is the off-diagonal part of the Gram, the part mean and variance never see.

How to hunt for your own 4d and 4e textures

  1. What mean and variance hold: per channel, how much and how variable. Nothing about which channels appear together. A texture is safe for mean_var when its look is carried by amounts: overall colour, contrast, fine grain with no particular shape.
  2. What only the Gram holds: co-occurrence. A texture needs it when its look depends on features appearing together: an edge with a particular colour on each side, strokes of a particular orientation, blobs with outlines.
  3. Predict, then run both. Pick a candidate, write down which loss you expect to fail and why, then check. The scramble toy in section 2 is the test in miniature.
  4. “Non-trivial” rules out flat colours and pure noise. Judge by eye, as the question says “looks acceptable”, and say what you looked at.

5 · question 4c · the start image

Same loss, same steps, three different starting points

The notebook starts from torch.randn: every pixel drawn from a Gaussian with mean 0 and standard deviation 1, so about half the values are negative and many are above 1, far outside the range of any image. The loss is non-convex, so where you start changes where you end W2 §6.4. Three starts for the generated colour texture, all with the Gram loss.

The question says to think about what you have implemented so far. Things you already have: the exemplar's own colour statistics, a Gaussian filter (Q3), and feature statistics (4a). I show two options and their measured effect; choosing and justifying one is your answer.

6 · question 4f · regular patterns

Why a Gram matrix cannot lay bricks

A regular pattern is defined by where things are relative to each other over long distances: every brick the same width, every joint lined up. The Gram matrix sums over positions, so the only spatial relations it keeps are those inside one feature's receptive field. At conv4_1 that is 68 pixels in this setup; at conv1_1 it is 3.

Reading the second row. It is the amplitude of the 2-D Fourier transform W4 §1.1, centre = low frequency. A periodic image puts its energy into a few sharp dots, one per repeat distance and direction. Your notes: the transform isolates “macro structures in low frequencies and fine details in high frequencies”. If a synthesised image has the right dots, it has the right repeat.
Published fixes you can research (the question asks for your own research and explanation): add a loss on the Fourier spectrum (Liu, Gousseau & Xia, 2016); add Gram matrices between features and spatially shifted copies of themselves (Berger & Memisevic, 2016); add a loss on feature autocorrelations (Sendik & Cohen-Or, 2017). All three put back a statistic that depends on relative position. The demo tries the first two.
